title: Weiqi Overview
audience: readers who want a first structural map of weiqi before studying joseki, life and death, or advanced strategy
goal: explain how liberties, capture, territory, and ko organize play in weiqi
_orderingNote: Each source lesson's own 'What comes next' section cross-links the others as a small graph, not a single line (e.g. living-groups-and-eyes points first to weiqi-history, weiqi-history points first back to living-groups-and-eyes). This 'next' chain picks one linear reading order — overview, living-groups-and-eyes, weiqi-history, komi-and-handicap, back to overview — using each lesson's first-listed 'next' pointer where that pointer is not already used earlier in the chain.

steps.text: Weiqi is a two-player territorial board game played by placing black and white stones on grid intersections, usually on a 19x19 board. Black moves first. Stones normally remain where they are played unless they are captured. Because the board state is almost fully public, the game rewards long-range spatial judgment rather than hidden-information inference.

Worked example: surrounding one stone. Black places one stone near the center of an empty 9x9 board. White then places a stone on each of the four points adjacent to it. Once Black's stone has no remaining liberties, White removes it from the board — a capture.
steps._comment: Position derived from weiqi-overview.md's 'Worked example: surrounding one stone': Black plays one stone near the center of an empty 9x9 board, White occupies each of its four orthogonal neighbors in turn, and the last of those White moves removes Black's last liberty. Center of a 9x9 board (columns A-H,J skip-I; rows 1-9, row 1 top) is E5, so its four neighbors are D5 (west), F5 (east), E4 (north, lower row number = top), E6 (south). The sequence below was replayed move-by-move through the built kernel (public/lib/kernel/index.mjs), with Black passing between White's placements so the moves stay strictly alternating and legal; it plays cleanly and the final White move reports capture/group-killed events, matching the lesson text exactly. Final stones and markers reflect that verified end state.

sequence.note: Black plays one stone near the center of an empty board.
Black passes, to let White's four-sided approach play out.
White approaches from the north. Black's stone now has one liberty left.
White's fourth stone removes Black's last liberty. Black's stone is captured and lifted from the board.

steps.text: This small example shows the core logic of the game. Stones do not move after placement. They remain in place, connect to neighboring stones of the same color, and survive only while their group retains at least one liberty. Much of weiqi can be understood as managing the relation between extension and enclosure. The central tactical unit is the liberty: a single stone in open space has four liberties, fewer on the edge, and fewer again in the corner. Connected stones share liberties, which is why groups matter more than isolated stones. A stone or group reduced to one liberty is in atari, the game's simplest tactical alarm.

The strategic objective is territory, not only capture. Players try to secure vacant points by surrounding them more solidly than the opponent can invade or reduce. This is why a move that does not capture anything immediately can still be strong: it may stabilize a large territorial framework or prevent the opponent from doing so.

The game also needs a rule to prevent immediate infinite repetition. That rule is ko: after a capture that would allow the opponent to recreate the exact previous board position with one move, that immediate recapture is forbidden. Ko turns some local fights into timing problems that reach across the whole board, because the player who is blocked from recapturing must play elsewhere first.
Why is a group of connected stones usually stronger than the same number of isolated stones?

exercise.prompt: Why is a group of connected stones usually stronger than the same number of isolated stones?
exercise.answerText: Connected stones share liberties. That usually makes them harder to capture because the opponent must remove the liberties of the whole group, not each stone separately.

steps.text: Why is ko important even though it applies only to a narrow kind of local repetition?

exercise.prompt: Why is ko important even though it applies only to a narrow kind of local repetition?
exercise.answerText: Without ko, some local captures could repeat forever and stop the game from progressing. Ko forces the fight to break and often links a local struggle to the wider board because one player must play elsewhere first.

title: Living Groups and Eyes
audience: readers who already understand liberties, capture, territory, and ko
goal: explain why connection and eye shape determine whether a group lives or dies

steps.text: Worked example: a corner group with two eyes. Black has enclosed a small corner group so that two separate empty points remain inside its shape. White surrounds the outside completely. Even so, Black's group is safe: White cannot fill both internal points, because each one functions as an eye, and the group stays alive as long as those internal liberties remain structurally separate.
steps._comment: Position derived from living-groups-and-eyes.md's 'Worked example: a corner group with two eyes': a small Black corner group with two separate internal empty points (eyes), fully surrounded on the outside by White. Realized concretely in the board's actual top-left corner (columns A-E, rows 1-3; row 1 is the top edge) as a minimal six-stone Black wall — A2, B1, B2, C2, D1, D2 — around two non-adjacent eye points A1 and C1, with a seven-stone White wall — A3, B3, C3, D3, E1, E2, E3 — sealing the outside. Verified two ways through the built kernel: (1) the Black group's only liberties are A1 and C1 (every other neighbor is Black or White, so nothing else keeps the group alive); (2) the whole position is reachable by a legal alternating game (A2,A3,B1,B3,B2,C3,C2,D3,D1,E1,D2,E2,pass,E3), after which White's isLegal("A1") and isLegal("C1") both report false — White genuinely cannot fill either eye, exactly as the lesson claims.

steps.text: This example shows why raw stone count is not enough. A surrounded group can still live if its shape is strong enough. In weiqi, survival depends less on "having many stones" than on building a form the opponent cannot legally or efficiently eliminate.

Connection makes groups stronger. A connection turns separate stones into one unit. That matters because connected stones share liberties, answer attacks together, and can build internal shape more efficiently than isolated stones can. Many local fights are really fights over cutting and connecting. When a player connects two weak stones, the move may look passive, but it often changes the status of the whole position: a connected group may escape atari, threaten to make eyes, or stop the opponent from splitting the board into easy targets.

Eyes and life. An eye is a protected empty point inside a group's shape. Under common rules, the opponent cannot simply play into a true eye if that move would leave the played stone without liberties and capture nothing. That is why eye shape matters so much. The usual practical rule is simple: a group with two secure eyes lives, while a group that cannot make two eyes may die. This is the core of life and death — players read local sequences to determine whether a group can form those eyes before the opponent seals it in.

Why this matters for the whole board. Life-and-death judgment is not a narrow endgame skill; it changes strategic value across the whole board. A move that saves a living group can preserve a large territorial framework. A move that kills an invading group can turn a contested region into secure territory. This is why advanced weiqi still returns to local shape: whole-board strategy decides where to fight, but life-and-death reading decides whether the stones in that fight can remain on the board.
Why is a connected group usually stronger than the same stones scattered apart?

exercise.prompt: Why is a connected group usually stronger than the same stones scattered apart?
exercise.answerText: Connected stones share liberties, defend each other, and can build eyes as one unit. Scattered stones can be cut apart and attacked separately.

steps.text: Why does the phrase "two eyes live" matter more than raw stone count?

exercise.prompt: Why does the phrase "two eyes live" matter more than raw stone count?
exercise.answerText: A group survives by preserving secure internal liberties, not by merely having many stones. Two proper eyes usually make capture impossible under ordinary play.

title: History of Weiqi
audience: readers who have followed the structural lessons and want institutional and historical context for weiqi
goal: trace how weiqi spread from its origins in China across East Asia and into global play while keeping its core rules intact
_comment: weiqi-history.md has no explicit 'Audience:' / 'Learning goal:' lines like the other three lessons do (it opens directly with prose instead). audience/goal above are this extraction's own summary of the lesson's content, not a quotation from the source.

steps.text: Weiqi's history is a long record of transmission and institutional refinement: a game that began in China, spread across East Asia, and later became a global competitive and educational tradition.

One game, three names. The same game is commonly called weiqi in Chinese, baduk in Korean, and go in Japanese-derived English usage. Those names mark more than translation — they show the route by which the game moved across linguistic and institutional settings while keeping a recognizable rules core.

Origins in China. The game originated in China more than two millennia ago, and some accounts place it much earlier. Early Chinese traditions treated it not only as recreation but as a cultivated art associated with scholarly accomplishment. What matters historically is durability: weiqi kept the same basic logic of placement, enclosure, and capture across centuries even as rule explanations, board conventions, and social settings changed.

Transmission across East Asia. Weiqi spread from China to Korea and Japan, where it developed strong local traditions and institutions. Japanese professional houses later played a major role in codifying teaching lineages, recording famous games, and circulating the name go beyond Japan. This transmission changed how the game was taught and organized, but not its basic identity: the core mechanics remained territorial placement, capture, and shape judgment. The major historical shifts were institutional and cultural rather than mechanical.

Modern international play. In the twentieth century, weiqi expanded far beyond East Asia through national associations, translated teaching materials, and international federations. That growth made rank systems, tournament rules, and teaching methods more legible to new players outside the game's older centers. Organizations outside East Asia often present handicap play as a normal and valuable part of the game, not as a lesser version of it — an emphasis that helped weiqi travel as both a competitive discipline and a teachable social practice.
What does the existence of the names weiqi, baduk, and go show about the game's history?

exercise.prompt: What does the existence of the names weiqi, baduk, and go show about the game's history?
exercise.answerText: It shows that the game spread across different linguistic and institutional settings while preserving a recognizable core structure.

steps.text: What changed most as weiqi spread internationally: its basic mechanics or its institutions of teaching and competition?

exercise.prompt: What changed most as weiqi spread internationally: its basic mechanics or its institutions of teaching and competition?
exercise.answerText: Its institutions changed more than its basic mechanics. The game kept the same territorial placement logic while different regions developed their own teaching systems, organizations, and naming traditions.

title: Komi and Handicap
audience: readers who understand basic weiqi structure and want to know how even games and uneven games are balanced
goal: explain the difference between komi and handicap, and show why weiqi uses both
_comment: This lesson's 'Worked example: even game versus teaching game' section is entirely about scoring/procedure (what komi and handicap are for), not a describable board position — it names no points or stone counts. Per the extraction brief ('where a lesson describes a position in prose, realize it concretely'), no 'board' step was fabricated for it; the worked example is carried as a 'read' step instead, faithfully to the source.

steps.text: Worked example: even game versus teaching game. In an even game, Black moves first and White receives komi, a fixed score bonus that offsets the first-move advantage. In a teaching game between players of unequal strength, the weaker player may instead receive handicap stones before play begins. These two adjustments solve different problems: komi balances the initiative inside an otherwise equal game, while handicap balances the starting position between unequal players.

Why komi exists. Weiqi is not fully symmetrical at the start because Black moves first. Komi compensates for that structural advantage by adding points to White's final score. This means the core rules of play stay the same while the scoring system absorbs the asymmetry. Komi therefore belongs to scoring, not to local tactics — it matters when the final territory and related points are counted, not when players are reading captures or life-and-death fights.

Why handicap exists. Handicap solves a different problem: it lets players of unequal strength compete in a game that still produces meaningful decisions for both sides. Instead of changing how stones move or how groups live, handicap changes the starting position by placing extra Black stones on the board before the first move. This matters pedagogically as well as competitively — a weaker player can experience middle-game and endgame decisions from a stronger position without needing the rules themselves to change.

Komi and handicap are not interchangeable. Komi is a scoring offset in an even game. Handicap is a positional offset in an uneven game. They should not be collapsed into one idea just because both are balancing devices. The difference matters because each adjustment shapes play differently: komi leaves the opening empty and symmetrical except for move order, while handicap creates immediate whole-board structure before ordinary play begins.
Why does komi affect the end of the game rather than the start of the board position?

exercise.prompt: Why does komi affect the end of the game rather than the start of the board position?
exercise.answerText: Because komi is a score adjustment, not an extra stone or changed move rule. It offsets Black's first move by changing the final count, not by altering local tactical play.

steps.text: Why is handicap useful even though komi already exists?

exercise.prompt: Why is handicap useful even though komi already exists?
exercise.answerText: Because komi balances even games, while handicap balances games between players of different strength. They address different asymmetries.
